title: The slave who went forth
hookLine: the first fruit: a slave who ordains is greeted with honor by the king himself

lines: A QUESTION ABOUT THE KING'S HOUSEHOLD.
cards: The king has asked his question: what fruit does the contemplative life bring, visible here and now? The Buddha could answer with a lecture on meditation, or freedom, or the end of suffering. He doesn't.
He answers with a question about the people in the king's own household. Great king, suppose there were a man in your service. Not a minister, not a guard.

teach.h: UP BEFORE THE KING, TO BED AFTER
teach.b: He gets up before you and goes to bed after you. He does whatever you want, speaks to please you, and watches your face for your mood. And one day he thinks: this is strange.

teach.h: HE IS HUMAN, AND SO AM I
teach.b: King Ajatasattu is a human being, and so am I. He lives like a god, and I live like this. Let me do something good with my life.
Let me shave my head, put on the ochre robe, and go forth. And he does. He lives restrained in body, speech and mind, content with simple food and shelter, glad to be alone.
Now suppose your people told you about him.

teach.h: WOULD YOU MAKE HIM A SLAVE AGAIN?
teach.b: Would you say: bring him back, make him my slave again?

teach.h: THE KING WOULD RISE FOR HIM
teach.b: And the king answers, honestly: no, lord. We would bow to him, stand up when he came, offer him a seat, robes, food, a place to live and medicine, and see that he was protected.
Then, the Buddha says, isn't that a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now? Yes, says the king. It is.
That's the first fruit: samaññaphala. The Buddha goes on to a free farmer who pays his taxes, with the same result.
Notice what the answer does. The king's own society, built on rank, already admits that this life changes how a person is seen. The man who watched the king's face now has the king rising for him.
It doesn't erase the cruelty of that world. But inside it, a door opens, and the king himself can see it.

how: In Buddhist monastic communities, seniority is counted from the day of ordination rather than from birth or former status, and lay people of every rank bow to monastics, including kings in some Theravada countries.

o: the fruit of the contemplative life
the reward a king gives loyal servants
a vow to own nothing at all

games.q: the slave who went forth: tap the pairs.
p: he is human, and so am I
we would rise and honor him
the fruit of the contemplative life
a free farmer who pays his taxes

s: the Buddha's first answer to the king is a lecture on meditation
it's a question about a slave in the king's own household.
the king admits he would honor the man who went forth
he'd rise for him, offer a seat, robes, food, lodging, medicine and protection.
the discourse says the slave's ordination ends slavery in the kingdom
it shows a door opening for one person inside a cruel system, and the king admitting it.

games.q: you're the king. your people tell you a man who was once your slave has gone forth and lives a restrained, simple life. what do you say?
o: we would bow and rise for him, and offer him what he needs.
let him be, but give him nothing.
games.why: the king answers honestly that he would honor him, and the Buddha points out: that's a fruit you can see, here and now.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose work goes unseen, someone who cleans, delivers, cooks or cares, who gets up before you and goes to bed after. Picture their face, and let the thought arise: this is a human being, and so am I.

wordCard.voice: Samannaphala. The fruit of the contemplative life: the first one, visible here and now, when a person once owned is honored even by the king.

orig.note: Pali samañña: the contemplative life; phala: fruit. the title of DN 2.

carryVoice: Your line: honored. The first fruit, and the king named it himself. Day five hundred twenty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (the fruits of the contemplative life), the first visible fruit
